title: Will the US and Iran return to war?
gist: Chatham House argues the US blockade of Iranian oil via Hormuz has hurt Iran's finances but is unlikely to win concessions, and may provoke Iran to lash out as in 2019 against Gulf energy infrastructure. China's oil purchases and Iran's defiant founding narrative sustain it; the author sees phased diplomacy (partial blockade relief for Hormuz reopening, then nuclear talks) as the only exit.

insights.claim: Resumption of US-Iran war is not solely Trump's call: Iran may itself reignite the conflict in an attempt to break the US naval blockade.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Tail risk of renewed Gulf conflict stays live even if Washington stands down.
insights.quote: Iran may also reignite the conflict, in an attempt to break the US blockade.
insights.locator: Will the US and Iran return to war?

insights.claim: Post-midterm speculation about new US strikes on Iran has not resolved; Trump said in a 60 Minutes interview he saw no reason to escalate, leaving Washington's next move unclear.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Policy signal leans toward continued economic pressure rather than renewed strikes, but is not binding.

insights.claim: Even if Trump keeps to economic strangulation rather than military operations, a return to armed conflict cannot be ruled out because Tehran is unlikely to absorb pressure quietly as its economy deteriorates.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not treat a US pause as de-escalation; the trigger may be Iranian.
insights.locator: It is possible that the president

insights.claim: The author expects Iran to resort to violence at some point to force Washington to reconsider the blockade, but that this is unlikely to succeed because the US also has its pride and interests.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect an Iranian escalation followed by a US doubling-down, i.e. return to square one.
insights.quote: Iran will at some point resort to violence to try to force Washington to reconsider.
insights.locator: But it still has to address the blockade

insights.claim: The US naval blockade of Iranian oil exports via Hormuz has evolved: launched in April, eased after the June MoU that reopened the Strait, and reinstated on 14 July as the deal unravelled.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Hormuz flows have been policy-dependent and reversible, so oil risk premia can swing with diplomacy.

insights.claim: The blockade has hurt Iranian finances, with some analyses indicating Iran loaded no oil onto tankers in September.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Iranian export volumes are near zero on some estimates, removing supply from the market.
insights.quote: Iran loaded no oil onto tankers in September

insights.claim: The blockade is unlikely to force significant Iranian concessions at the bargaining table and may instead push Tehran to lash out, taking all parties back to square one.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Economic pressure may raise rather than lower escalation risk.
insights.locator: This is the irony of the US naval blockade

insights.claim: The two sides are in a sequencing stalemate: Iran wants the blockade lifted and its conditions met before reopening Hormuz and stopping attacks, while Washington wants nuclear concessions before talks on maritime security.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Neither side can move first without a face-saving structure, so the status quo persists until a shock.

insights.claim: US officials believe the blockade is working and are doubling down, with US Central Command authorised to set up a new task force to prevent Iran using ground routes to transport advanced weapons.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The US is expanding rather than easing enforcement, reducing near-term odds of a blockade climbdown.

insights.claim: In 2019 Iran answered Trump's maximum pressure with attacks: tanker strikes near Fujairah and the Gulf of Oman in May-June, a downed US drone, and on 14 September drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and the Khurais oil field.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Precedent shows the response function: economic pressure leads to attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure, with no US strike on Iranian soil needed.

insights.claim: Tehran's 2019 message was that it will respond to extreme economic pressure by attacking Gulf energy infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gulf energy assets and shipping are the likely targets of any renewed Iranian lashing out.
insights.quote: We will respond to extreme economic pressure by attacking Gulf energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Iran's first reason for escalating is ideological: it is defending a founding narrative of sacrifice, endurance and defiance of outside pressure, which Washington fails to grasp.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Coercion that ignores regime identity will likely backfire.

insights.claim: The 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war, which Iran fought almost alone against a US- and Gulf-backed adversary and survived, makes a year or two of blockade hardship look comparatively mild to the regime.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Iran's pain tolerance and historical reference points are higher than Western models assume.

insights.claim: The second reason is practical: unlike in the Iraq war, Iranian defiance is now aided by outsiders, with China the biggest source of support through its purchases of Iranian oil.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China is the key swing actor sustaining Iranian staying power; Chinese demand for Iranian crude is a hinge for blockade outcomes.

insights.claim: Without China the regime's staying power would drastically diminish, which is why US officials have reportedly urged Beijing to play a more constructive role in ending the conflict.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch US-China diplomacy and Chinese oil purchases as leading indicators of blockade success.

insights.claim: Tehran is betting that the Gulf states most hurt by the crisis (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait) will press Washington harder to find an exit if Iran holds out long enough.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gulf lobbying of Washington is a possible path to blockade easing.

insights.claim: In 1988, after Operation Praying Mantis and months of losses, Khomeini accepted a ceasefire, likening it to drinking poison, showing Iran can concede when survival is at stake.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Iran has conceded under existential threat before, but the current situation is different.
insights.locator: There are limits to Iranian resilience

insights.claim: The blockade differs from 1988 because Iran could not have won then and continuing would likely have meant military collapse, whereas today Iran believes it has the upper hand and that it has already won, defining regime survival and avoiding a major US attack as victory.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A regime that sees itself as winning has little incentive to concede, raising the bar for any deal.

insights.claim: Some in the Iranian regime will judge it better to fight on Iran's own terms than to collapse from within as the economy is throttled, and doubt US concessions would be durable enough to bring lasting relief.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Mutual distrust raises the odds that internal hardliners favour escalation.

insights.claim: The only way out is phased diplomacy: first Washington partially lifts the blockade in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait and ceasing all attacks on shipping; second, nuclear talks with gradual sanctions lifting and release of frozen Iranian funds.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A phase-one deal would be the key catalyst for restored Hormuz flows and lower energy risk premia.

insights.claim: Both sides want to end the conflict but are determined to avoid perceived humiliation, and Israel remains an unpredictable factor, so it is not clear that sense will prevail.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Face-saving and Israeli action are the main spoilers for a deal.
